chase_cards.name: No.1 Trainer [World Challenge Secret Super Battle regional first place]
chase_cards.why: This is a chase because it is the senior-track champion's credential from the parallel World Challenge route: the player won a regional Secret Super Battle event and received a personalized No.1 Trainer that points toward Japan's own Best in Japan machinery, not the junior Tropical Mega Battle route.

key_artists.name: Ken Sugimori
examples: No.1 Trainer [World Challenge Secret Super Battle regional first place]
key_artists.why: Sugimori matters here because the senior-track trophy card is both a competitive credential and a franchise object. His artwork anchors the card in the same visual language that made early Pokémon recognizable before the tournament circuit had global polish.

claims.text: The local catalog models the World Challenge Secret Super Battle regional first-place source group as one row containing No.1 Trainer at source index 177.
Bulbapedia says No.1 Trainer began as a Japanese tournament Trainer card and later became a first-place prize in the Pokémon World Championships.

Bulbapedia says the World Challenge Summer 2000 No.1 Trainer iteration was first awarded to the champions of each regional Japanese World Challenge Summer event held between July and August 2000, with the circuit split into Tropical Mega Battle and Secret Super Battle events and retaining the age-limited structure.

Bulbapedia says top-ranking players from Secret Super Battle were eligible to compete in a Best in Japan Deciding Match in late August 2000, while overall winners of Tropical Mega Battle regional events represented Japan in the World Exchange Battle in Hawaii; this dossier does not treat Secret Super Battle regional first place as the Hawaii route.

Pokumon describes World Challenge Summer 2000 as a regional tournament circuit across eight Japanese venues, with the juniors championship known as Tropical Mega Battle and the senior-player counterpart as Secret Super Battle Best in Japan.

Pokumon says the card text distinguished Tropical Mega Battle for players aged 14 or under from Secret Super Battle for players 15+, supporting the senior-track boundary for Secret Super Battle cards.
Bulbapedia says the World Challenge Summer 2000 No.1 Trainer cards were personalized with the winner's name and regional conference and were Non Holofoil.

Bulbapedia says two base versions of the World Challenge Summer 2000 No.1 Trainer exist, one depicting a male Trainer and the other a female Trainer, with the awarded version depending on the winner's gender.
Bulbapedia says the World Challenge Summer No.1 Trainer major iteration used new artwork by Ken Sugimori.

Bulbapedia describes Ken Sugimori as a friend of Satoshi Tajiri, illustrator of the original Pokémon game artwork, illustrator of TCG cards and merchandise, and the artist who redrew all 151 Generation I Pokémon in watercolor for promotional use.

Pokumon says Secret Super Battle Best in Japan was held at Pokémon Center Tokyo on August 19, 2000 and that winners of that final event received No.1-3 Trainer trophy cards that are reported to be cosmos holofoil with the winner's photograph printed onto them, but that no photos have surfaced to confirm that report.

Pokumon identifies Boy SSB No.1 Trainer and Girl SSB No.1 Trainer as World Challenge Secret Super Battle 2000 regional first-place prizes, Japanese unnumbered non-holo Trainer Winner cards illustrated by Ken Sugimori, and gives estimated copy counts for each gendered version; this dossier treats those counts as collector estimates, not official disclosure.

As judged collector texture, the regional Secret Super Battle No.1 Trainer matters because it is the senior-track champion credential: not the Hawaii-bound junior route, not a final-stage photo trophy, but a personalized regional win in the older-player circuit.

narrative.human_title: No.1 Trainer [World Challenge Secret Super Battle regional]: the senior-track champion card
narrative.why_it_matters: This No.1 Trainer is a different kind of first place than the Tropical Mega Battle version. It belongs to Secret Super Battle, the older-player track, so the card feels less like a passport to Hawaii and more like a regional crown inside Japan's senior competitive circuit. The personalization matters: name, conference, gendered base art, and Sugimori artwork turn a tournament result into a durable object. It is not merely a trophy label; it is evidence that Pokémon's early organized play was already splitting age, route, rank, and memory into precise printed forms.
not_claiming: that every No.1 Trainer listing uses this same route

special_identification_instructions.trigger: Use when a card, listing, slab label, auction description, or agent claim says No.1 Trainer, World Challenge, Secret Super Battle, SSB, regional first place, senior division, 15+, personalized name, Best in Japan, photo trophy, or Tropical Mega Battle.
special_identification_instructions.summary: Treat No.1 Trainer as a reusable trophy-card title. Establish the Secret Super Battle regional route before comparing value, rarity, or historical meaning.
steps: Confirm the card is No.1 Trainer / Ｎｏ.１トレーナー and that the claimed promotion is World Challenge Secret Super Battle regional first-place prize, not Tropical Mega Battle, Secret Super Battle Best in Japan, Challenge Road '99, Lizardon Mega Battle, Kamex Mega Battle, Neo Road, Battle Road, or World Championships.

Check whether the card is the 2000 World Challenge Summer regional Secret Super Battle version: non-holo, personalized with winner name and regional conference, and based on male or female Trainer artwork depending on winner gender.
Keep the age-route split legible: Pokumon describes Tropical Mega Battle as for players aged 14 or under and Secret Super Battle as for players 15+.
Do not treat Secret Super Battle regional first place as the Hawaii representative slot. Bulbapedia assigns the Hawaii / World Exchange Battle path to overall Tropical Mega Battle regional winners.

Separate this regional non-holo card from Secret Super Battle Best in Japan final cards, which Pokumon reports as possible cosmos holofoil photo trophies and explicitly marks as unconfirmed by surfaced photos.
Record Pokumon gendered-version copy counts only as collector estimates. Do not convert them into official print-run facts.

Before spending or trade gating, require seller-controlled photos of the actual card, including name/conference personalization, front/back, surface, edge, and slab label if graded; catalog identity is legible support, not physical truth.
not_claiming: that No.1 Trainer name alone identifies the exact print
that a grading label alone resolves the route

claims.text: The local catalog row identifies source index 177 as No.1 Trainer from the World Challenge Secret Super Battle regional first-place prize slice.

As interpretive art context, Sugimori's credit gives this senior-track first-place card the same visual authority as the junior-track trophy cards while the event text and route distinguish its competitive meaning.

This card must be separated from World Challenge Tropical Mega Battle regional No.1 Trainer, Secret Super Battle Best in Japan No.1 Trainer, Challenge Road '99, Lizardon Mega Battle, Kamex Mega Battle, Neo Road, Battle Road, World Championships No.1 Trainer, and name-only No.1 Trainer listings.

As judged collector texture, No.1 Trainer [World Challenge Secret Super Battle regional first place] is interesting because it preserves the older-player regional champion role: parallel to the famous TMB lane, but not swallowed by it.

narrative.human_title: No.1 Trainer: the senior-track champion, not the Hawaii myth
narrative.why_it_matters: This is where the No.1 Trainer name has to be handled with real respect. The card sounds like every other first-place trophy until the route is read closely: Secret Super Battle, older players, regional champion, Best in Japan track. That makes it perfect for the catalog because the name is not enough. The assembly is the meaning.
not_claiming: that every No.1 Trainer print follows this route
